title: A built-in table is just a table
lede: Communities can already create tables that declare everything about themselves — fields, states, presentation — as data they can see and edit. The tables the app ships with cannot: a built-in's base fields, states, order, presentation and capabilities still live in code, where only a deploy can change them. The canonical plan (docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md) already collapsed forms and tables into one catalog with one generic mount, and inventory is cut over — the template for every hardcoded table (docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md). What remains is the declaration itself. The journey ends when "built-in" is only where the seed came from — and, per the plan's subtraction rule, when the old hardcoded paths are deleted, not merely bypassed.
callout: Giving built-in tables the write vocabulary community tables already had (gh#1870) turned the promotion gate red, on exactly the fault line docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §5 warned about: builtins are EXEMPT from `tables:<id>` names and keep their URL-mirroring names — "pin it with a test". That seam belongs to the permissions journey, which now carries the standing enforced-equals-grantable check (gh#1944) that would have caught it on the change rather than on the release. The rule for this epic: when a step here moves a permission surface, it plugs into that seam instead of minting a parallel one.

steps.title: A table says what its own base fields are
steps.body: Everything below depends on this — docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §3c states it as the first invariant: "one field vocabulary is the contract between form-side and table-side... get it right first; everything composes against it." Today a built-in's base columns — title, status, the state values — live in code, while a community table declares all of it as data in the one catalog (the generalized form_definitions, per that doc's Resolved decision 2). gh#1836 makes the base fields visible and declarable, and makes `status` optional with per-table values. gh#1851 was this landing badly the first time: the built-in seed kept a status column the new base-field block forbade, and development went red until the seed was allowed to keep the column it describes.

steps.title: The declared state survives being edited
steps.body: A state list you can edit is a state list you can break — and the plan's quality bar (docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §1b-E) says no slice ships a regression for existing communities. gh#1844 is the sharp edge: delete a row state and its stored value can be re-minted later by a different state, silently re-pointing any practice criterion that named it — the practice keeps matching, on rows it was never about. gh#1845 is the quieter half: the submission usage-analytics counter compares against the hardcoded Approved/Rejected strings, so a table whose author replaced its states never fires it — authoring states costs the community its own numbers.

steps.title: A table declares how it presents itself
steps.body: Order, columns, widgets. gh#1837 lets a table declare its default row order. gh#1877 shows the row state as a column and wires the place widget to built-in tables. gh#1862 gives built-in table settings the show/hide switch a custom table has — the /settings/tables surface docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §5 specifies (rename, show/hide, permissions, delete). Direction check from the docs: column configuration belongs in the ONE definition's per-field `listColumn` (docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §3b) — the inventory cutover deliberately DROPPED the bespoke column picker for exactly that reason (docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md). So each of these must land as catalog data, not as another code-side overlay.

steps.title: A field declares its own limits, and the server believes only the declaration
steps.body: gh#1874: a number field states its bounds and the server enforces them — at the ONE gated write seat, which is where the canonical plan puts all submission validation (`createSubmissionGated` + `validateSubmissionAnswers`, docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md W2/E3c and §9a: every live create path is gated there). Worth doing here rather than in the form layer, because the same pattern already failed once elsewhere — gh#1684, the relations maxItems cap, is enforced only in the browser while treasury-summary trusts it on the server. A declared limit that only the client checks is not a limit.

steps.title: One action vocabulary, on the row and on the selection
steps.body: gh#1875 is the owner decision that a button is a button: one list of actions a table declares for its rows and for a multi-row selection. Today the only way to put a button on a row is a code presenter, and presenters are refused for community tables — inventory has a Reserve button no community table can have. The docs already frame the presenter as an overlay for what "the data definition can't carry" and the row accessor as an incremental-migration seam, not the end state (docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §3a; docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md §2) — gh#1875 moves actions from that seam into the declaration, following the existing fail-closed `crud` pattern (declaration ∧ permission). Adjacent bugs showing the surface is untended: gh#1770 (mobile View opens EDIT), gh#1763 (AppTable discards the caller's emptyState).

steps.title: Finance cuts over, and the old descriptors are deleted
steps.body: The strand this epic was missing, and the canonical plan's biggest open risk (docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §W5 subtraction ledger): transactions and reimbursements are seeded as builtins with row-sources and presenters, but their live routes still render the old descriptor — TWO definitions each, 593 duplicate lines, a live drift surface (gh#1395). The ledger is explicit about why this sits here and not earlier: the catalog copies lack createdBy, relations, bank-account/IBAN, approval metadata and import/export, so deletion is a functional completion of the declaration, which is what the steps above build. The plan's rule binds the whole epic: "a cutover slice is not done when the new path works. It is done when the old path is deleted." Inventory's S4 cutover is the template (docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md).

steps.title: Capabilities become per-table, and each carries its own permission
steps.body: gh#1838 turns discussion and history into per-table capabilities with a permission action each — today both render only for people who can EDIT the row, which is backwards for shared records. The pattern is already shipped and documented: community tables mint per-object runtime families (`tables:<id>:<action>`) merged through the ONE `getPermissionsForScope` seam, no second resolver (docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §2). Two traps that doc records from experience: a new verb must be added to the permission generator's ACTIONS set or the grant is silently dropped — a name nobody can hold, the same shape as gh#1870's enforced-but-ungrantable gap; and builtins keep their URL-mirroring names (`resources:inventory:*`), exempt from per-object names by design (§5) — the capability's permission must respect both namings.

steps.title: Sharing and row scoping reach built-in tables
steps.body: Table sharing is BUILT for community tables — docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §8 records T1–T7 all shipped 2026-08-05: grantable per-table tiers, the permissions modal, /settings/tables, `table_shares` with the owner-picked row scope (R6: none/self/community/all), recipient-side read through the gateway, pre-submit disclosure. Builtins are outside all of it: the doc notes their row-sources have no self-scope (a `read-self` holder is deliberately 404'd, §6.1), and gh#1870 left manage, share and import unlevelled for builtins. If a built-in table is just a table, the share modal and the SQL-level row tiers must work on a builtin's row-source too — while keeping the documented builtin naming exemption (§5) intact.

steps.title: What a row shows is a practice, not hidden code
steps.body: The last thing still living in code. gh#1841 makes row visibility practice-driven: whether an item appears depends on the table's practice, which a community can read and change. Two constraints from the docs. It composes with, not replaces, the who-axis that already exists — permission tier and share scope decide who may look, the practice decides what a looker sees (docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md). And the filter must hold at SQL level: that doc's §6.1 rejects in-memory row filtering because a trimmed page still leaks `totalCount` as a row-count oracle — the same bar applies to a practice-shaped filter. After this, a built-in table has nothing left a community table cannot express.

stepsFrom.projector: the paper reader in the roadmap this app was extracted from (src/modules/paper/steps.ts)
stepsFrom.why: This journey has a paper as well as the steps stored here. Where a roadmap is showing it, the sections of that paper are what a reader sees, and they may differ from these. This app holds and draws the stored ones; it cannot read the paper, so it cannot tell you where the two disagree.

exists: One catalog and one renderer, per docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md: the catalog IS the generalized form_definitions with source builtin|community; the /tables/:slug mount has full gated CRUD; the W1 field vocabulary is DONE and everything renders through one FieldControl.

The inventory cutover is DONE and is the named template for migrating any hardcoded table — /resources/inventory renders the same GenericTablePage as /tables/inventory (docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md, S4 landed 2026-07-23).

Table sharing v3 is BUILT for community tables: T1–T7 shipped, including SQL-level read-self, the one permissions modal, table_shares with owner-decided scope (R6), and the recipient-side read (docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §8). The Owner-lockout question is CLOSED — an Owner always reaches every table in their own community (§6.4).
The list toolbar convention (gh#1281) already owns action placement for both table shapes.

gh#1870 landed one table-level permission vocabulary for both kinds — deliberately leaving manage, share and import unlevelled for builtins, and with a follow-up red gate (gh#1889, gh#1890) in its wake.
missing: Nothing yet proves the two table kinds stay in step: the red gate behind gh#1889/gh#1890 fired only after merge, because PR checks never run the DB-backed suite guarding builtin grants — the comparison has to run before merge, which is what gh#1944 is for on the permissions journey. Structurally, the mount's builtin write surfaces were deliberately CLOSED (requireWritableTable 404s builtin slugs; createSubmissionGated refuses builtin formIds — docs/INVENTORY_CONVERGENCE.md), so this epic is knowingly reopening a documented decision and must update those seams, not route around them. Builtin row-sources have no read-self scope (docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §6.1), so sharing/row tiers cannot reach builtins yet (gh#1908). And transactions + reimbursements still carry two definitions each until gh#1395 — the docs' subtraction rule (old path deleted, not bypassed) is the epic's real finish line.

order.why: docs/FORMS_TABLES_UNIFICATION.md §3c: the field vocabulary is the contract — get it right first; everything else reads it.
An editable state list that corrupts practices is worse than a fixed one — the plan's no-regression bar (§1b-E).
Independent of each other; can go in parallel. All land as catalog data, not code overlays.
Needs the presentation layer settled; moves the presenter seam's last code-only capability into the declaration.
The W5 ledger blocks deletion on the declaration being complete — which the steps above deliver. Cutover is done when the old path is deleted.
These change the permission surface and the practice engine at once, and must plug into the shipped sharing/permission seams (docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md) rather than mint parallel ones.

open: Does a built-in table keep its seed identity after a community edits its base fields, or does it become an ordinary table with history?

gh#1840 lets a composed page replace a built-in leaf at the same address — the sections journey carries it. Is it the page-level twin of this journey, and does anything table-shaped fall out of it here?

When sharing reaches builtins: docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md §9 leaves open the default reach of a new table and whether a sub-community reaches a parent's table within a tree — both bite harder once builtins are ordinary tables.
Submission deletes still fire no rules (gh#1366, deleteSubmissionGated does not exist) — if row visibility becomes a practice (gh#1841), delete staying ungated is the adjacent hole.

quizzes.question: Why did the built-in status column break development in gh#1851?
options: The seed wrote a column the new base-field declaration did not allow it to keep
The column was renamed in the locale files but not in the schema
quizzes.why: Making base fields declarable also made them exclusive. The seed describes its own status column, so it has to be allowed to keep it — the fix was to permit the seed, not to drop the column.

quizzes.question: Per docs/TABLE_SHARING_DESIGN.md, which tables use `tables:<id>:action` permission names?
options: All tables — one naming for everything is the whole point
Community-created tables only; builtins keep URL-mirroring names like resources:inventory:read
Built-in tables only, since they exist at deploy time
quizzes.why: §5: requiring per-object grants for builtins would hide finance tables from every treasurer role on deploy. "One system" means community tables use per-object names and builtins keep their URL-mirroring names — the exemption gh#1870's vocabulary merge has to preserve.

vocabulary.means: A table the app itself seeds at deploy — inventory, transactions, reimbursements. "Built-in" does not mean fixed or untouchable: the whole journey is making it an ordinary table, so that built-in ends up meaning only where the seed came from.

A table a community creates for itself in the product. It already declares everything — fields, states, presentation — as data. It is the finish line built-ins are being walked toward, not a lesser kind of table.

The one database store holding every table's definition (the generalized form_definitions). Not a product catalog or a list of anything — when a step says something must "land as catalog data", it means the table's own stored definition, readable and editable by the community, instead of code.

A table describing itself as data in the catalog, as opposed to behavior hardcoded next to it. "Declares" is the load-bearing word of the epic: whatever is declared, a community can see and change; whatever stays in code, only a deploy can.

A column a table has from birth — title, status — before its author adds any of their own. For built-ins these still live in code; making them declarable (gh#1836) is the first step everything else composes against.

The per-table list of values a row moves through (Approved, Rejected, …), declared as data — not a fixed status enum. Because practices and counters name these values by string, editing the list can silently re-point what depends on it.

The two code-side seams a built-in still leans on: the presenter overlays rich cells the data definition can't carry (inventory's Reserve button), the row-source says where its rows actually live (a legacy table instead of submissions). Both are documented as migration seams, not the end state — each step drains something out of them into the declaration.

Deleting the old path, not just shipping the new one. A cutover slice counts as finished only when the code it replaced is gone — until then the app carries two definitions of the same table (transactions and reimbursements do today) and they drift.

The community's written decision about how things are done here (fi tapa, pl. tavat), paired with the action that runs it — the concept the practices journey owns. When a step says row visibility becomes "a practice", it means a stored decision the community can read, edit and switch off, instead of hidden code.
